projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site, "D-Day 2004" release, for the Veterans History Project, 5/15/2004.

samplingDecl.p: The entire interview with George Van Sant was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p:
This is Jen Feldman. I am conducting an interview with Mr. George Van Sant November 7, 2001. He was born on November
20, 1927. He currently lives at 1407 Washington Avenue,
Fredricksberg, Virginia. He served in the Korean and World War II, and he was in the U.S. Marine Corps.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Question: Were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p: A:I enlisted.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:What were you doing before you ended up serving?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:Well, I was -- this was in World War II, I was in college.
I had gotten to college fairly young. And the last couple of
years of the war, because I was large, big, and looked older,
lots of mothers used to ask me why I wasn't in the service.
And I'd have to explain I was too young. And finally I
prevailed upon my mother to sign the enlistment papers,
because I was enlisting under 18 I had to have her signature,
and she was reluctant to do it because my father at the time
was overseas as a Lend Lease Administrator in Chung King,
China, and so she really, well, there you go, I finally
prevailed upon her and I enlisted in July of 1945 was just
before the war ended, and I was sent to Paris Island.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:How old were you when you actually enlisted, were you 17?

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:And what made you join?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:Well, the atmosphere in war time America in World War II,
everybody went. The only people who were not serving were people who were 4F or people who had extremely critical job
skills that they had to stay, but everybody went. And, as I
say, my own father, who was really too old to serve in the
armed services, but he left before the war started. He left
his professorial job at Penn State and moved into, first of
all, in the War Production Board down in Washington in
federal government, and then he got sent overseas as a Lend
Lease Administrator; so everybody went. I wanted to get in, I really did.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:Why did you pick the Marine Corps?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p: A:Well, it was the most challenging.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:Most challenging?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:I guess. An old friend of mine had enlisted in it and
came back from boot camp and told me a bunch of stories about
Paris Island, and I thought it would be great.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p:
Q:I have a friend of mine who joined the Marines, and she
was down in Paris Island last spring. So what was both camp
like, training like?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:It's pretty awful. It was then, and I think they could do
things to us then that they are not allowed to now, but we --
it was very good training though. I mean you really -- it
really makes a very disciplined Marine out of you, and you
come out in tremendous physical shape, and you feel like you
can lick anybody.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:Since you served in two wars, where exactly did you serve in World War II, and then Korea?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:While I was at Parris Island in boot camp they dropped the
atomic bomb.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:Okay.

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:And so by the time I got out of boot camp the war already
had ended.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:Okay.

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:But, see, when I went to Parris Island they had more
Marines training there then they ever did in history.
Because the, as you know, the plans were already drawn, and
in fact I've seen the plans since, for the landings on Japan.
And we were being trained as replacements for those landings.
And replacements were cannon fodder. I mean, in fact the
drill instructors told us, "you listen to what we're telling
you because six months from now half of you are going to be
dead. So if you listen carefully and you learn what we teach
you maybe you'll be one of the lucky half." So in truth the
motivator. So naturally when the war ended I was pretty
happy, and, but the replacement draft that I was put in I
went overseas anyway. And I sailed down the east coast of
Panama, and then to Pearl Harbor, and then to North China.
The Marines landed in North China, which is -- and I was part
of that too. We took the surrender of the Japanese and
rounded up -- Japaneese had two million men in China at the
end of the war; and we rounded them up and repatriated them back to Japan, disarmed them, they surrendered. They were
very cooperative. And we actually helped liberate a couple
of prison camps over there; and the company I was with in
North China we actually escorted a whole bunch of mostly
European prisoners who had been -- some of them had been in
prison camps for six or seven years since before World War II
started because the Japanese-Chinese War started in 1937 out
there. And we took them to the coast and got them aboard a
ship and they were sent back to Europe. So I did a lot of
interesting things in China; and of course the civil war was
going on over there between the communists and the
nationalists. And I kind of got a ringside seat on that. In
fact I got shot at a couple of times.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:When did you go to Korea, was that right in the beginning?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:No. I came back from China, was discharged and enlisted
in the reserve. I came back, I was a sergeant when I came
back from China, I enlisted in the reserve to save my
stripes, and then went back, finished college, went to work
and worked a couple of years and the Korean War came along in
1950 and I was called back in as a sergeant.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:Okay.

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:But because I finished college I didn't get to Korea until
a year and a half after the war started. But I came up here
to Quantico, went through Officer Candidate School, became a
second lieutenant, then went out to the west coast and on to Korea and got into the same regiment I had been in in China.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:And were you there until 1953 when it ended?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:I went over in April '52 and came home in April '53. I
was there for almost the whole last year of the war. But I,
believe it or not, there was a lot of combat in Korea during
that year, and I saw I had a rifle put ____

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:Were there many casualties in your unit?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:Yes. Lots of them. The company I went with was Fox Company, Second Battalion, 1st Marines. Between the time I
joined the company -- the company had seven officers; between
the time I joined the company and by the time I came home we
had had twenty-five officers. Company has 221 enlisted men,
we had had 540. That means the rest were killed and wounded,
and that's wounded and evacuated. So, yes, we did. We had
several minor battles, but we were engaged in one battle
that's still listed on the calendar, and that's Bunker Hill
in Korea. I was on Bunker Hill the whole time.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p:
Q:What are some of your most memorable experiences from
serving in Korea?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:Well, it was -- I was scared most of the time, and but
when you are a platoon commander you have a lot of
responsibility, and you have to look after your men; and I
formed some bonds and friendships over there, some of which I
still maintain.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:I see on your form that you were awarded a couple over medals and citations. Can you explain how you received them?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:Well, the Bronze Star was for -- it was called Meritorious
Bronze Star for valor. And the main thing it was for I once
led my platoon on a raid into the Chinese trench line.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p:
Q:And while you were gone how did you stay in touch with
your family?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p: A:By letter.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:By letter?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p: A:Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:Were you married when you --

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:Well, that was one of the main reasons I went to Korea was
because I had been -- I was married after I finished college
in 1948, and about a year and a half, almost two years after,
my wife contracted Tuberculosis, which was a very wide spread
disease back in the 40's. And she had -- and she diagnosed
when I got called back into the Marine Corps in 1950, and so
they kept me in the states, and in fact when I came up to
Quantico to go to Officer Candidate School why most of my
class fellow officers were sent right over to Korea, but they
kept me here because of her situation, she was in a
sanatorium, and not doing well, and in October of '51, she
died. So I had no wife when I was over there. But she -- it
was kind of sad because she was -- as she was in the
sanatorium they were developing a cure for Tuberculosis.
There was a drug that cured it, the doctors kept telling me that it's a race, if they can get this drug, and get it to
where we can give it to her and it might clear it up. She
was one of the last people in America to die of TB.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:Really. What was the food like?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p: A:In the Marine Corps?

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:Yeah.

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:Well, it varied. Sometimes it was very good. Sometimes
it was awful. Food at Parris Island and boot camp was
excellent. They gave you all you wanted to eat. I mean,
believe it or not, I was running and climbing obstacles and
doing everything in the world and I gained 16 pounds, and,
but it was all muscle, and, but the food was good. In 1950,
when I was called back, see the Marine Corps went almost
overnight from, I think, let's see, they had I believe when
the Korean War started the Marine Corps had something like
70,000 people on active duty. They mobilized the entire
reserve, the Marine Corps more than doubled within about a
month and a half, and the food the first few months after I
got called back was just awful. Well, the cooks and the
bakers they were all called back from civilian life where
they were probably cab drivers or something else like that.
And they when I was still a sergeant when ________ in Camp Lajeune, and I had a work party one time and I went to work
to help the mess hall and we were breaking out shipping
frozen meat in for the butcher in the mess hall. This meat was frozen, we were carrying it, it's whole sides of beef,
you know what a side of beef looks like, takes a couple of
people to carry it.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:Yeah.

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:And stamped on the beef, this meat had been frozen in
1944. This was 1950, six years later. Believe me the meat
was -- in fact meats all tasted the same. Pork -- they all
tasted the same because it was all so old. So it was
retched (sic). And of course, in combat, and in Korea the food
______ pretty much.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p:
Q:Did you do anything for good luck? Did you have any
special ritual or anything?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:That's an interesting question. I'm just trying to think.
Well, before I went in, in fact the year before I went in in
1944, my mother gave me a prayer book, I'm an Episcopalian,
and I always carried that prayer book with me, and I still
have it. I guess that and I -- oh, I carried a couple of
lucky nickels I think for a while _______...(4 seconds)

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p:
Q:How did you entertain yourself when you weren't in combat
and doing your other assignments and jobs?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:Well, you wrote a lot of letters, you read a lot, and when
I was an officer in Korea -- let's see, I was an enlisted man
in China. China was great because we were stationed in the
big city, Tianjin in North China, which is near Peking --
near Bejing, which it's called now, and I traveled a good deal in North China. I saw a lot of the country when I was
there, and on duty. I mean I was official, but we had
liberty in Tianjin. And there they were nice, there were
restaurants, and dance halls and bars and places to go,
things to do, and movie theaters and things likes that. In
Korea, when we -- quite frankly, when you -- the way it was
rotation, we had three regiments in the division. Two were
always on line and one was in reserve. Now, when you were in
reserve you were in camps behind the line. You trained, but
you also rested and you got showers, and you got clean
uniforms, and you got kind of fixed up, and you absorbed
replacements, and that or sort of thing. And you'd go in
reserve for a month and then you would spend two months on
line and then you'd come back for another month off. And
that when you first came back off line, first of all, the
unit would always be down in strength because of the
casualties. You wouldn't have as many men. And you were
just worn out. I mean on line you were on fifty percent
watch all night. Which meant you only slept half the night
and the rest of the time _____. As an officer I mean I
always checked on my troops all the time at night. I got
probably less than half a nights sleep. You were just worn
out. We'd usually kind of pitch about a 36 hour binge,
because we weren't allowed to drink on line, and come back
and quite frankly did a lot of heavy drinking. Particularly when we first got off. And we'd play cards. And when I was
an officer we had for quite a while in our battalion we had a
nice singing group, and we used to sing.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:Are there any humorous or unusual events you experienced?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p: A:Oh, my God, a million of them.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:Feel free too give a few.

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:Well, it's kind of interesting because I'm -- I went in in
'45 and I was out for a while, finished college, and then
went back in and got out in '53. Then I went to grad school
and finished and got my Phd in '58, and came here. I've been
here since '58, on faculty here. And but until '77 _____I
had -- the Marine Corps used to activate me for three months
every year. So I'd spend nine months teaching and three
months on active duty with the Marine Corps. That's how I
got all the way up to colonel. And they sent me all over the
world for things in the summer times. But, so I had a kind
of a reserve career almost in 32 years in the Marine Corps.
But I was starting to tell you, oh, yeah, that eight years
from '45 to '53 when I was really active and overseas twice,
I've written a memoir about it, and I've the draft finished.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:Really.

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:And my wife is helping me tremendously. I dictate and she
transcribes. So I have filled that with a lot of funny
anecdotes and things, crazy things that happened. There's so
many of them I'm trying too make a selection, but, well, I'll tell you one that I hope I can explain it so that it makes
sense. When the war ended and we went over in North China, I
was a private then, I had big feet. They issued -- we didn't
have boots in those days we had a kind of a low quarter shoe.
It came up to here about, and then we wore leggins (sic); remember
leggins, you've seen leggins?

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:Yeah.

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:Old fashioned leggins; well we wore leggins. A lot of the
men's boots wore out in North China, and we were thrown in
there, we just landed in there, and occupied the country, but
our supply line was not that well set up. And, you know, you
couldn't get replacement boots, and it really got to be
critical. In fact, a lot of the guys in the outfit had worn
away holes, like bums, in the bottom of their boots, and
were putting cardboard, we put cardboard inserts in the
bottom of your shoe to keep going because there was no
replacement boots. Well, it became a critical matter and we
had a regimental inspection at one time, and the colonel who
inspected our regiment, very formal inspection, and he -- I
don't know if you've seen a military platoon being inspected
in any way, he came up to our first platoon, which was -- we
were all lined up, one big line, three lines actually, but
covered a huge front. He comes to the very first outfit and
he goes down and inspects the rifles of everybody in the
squad, and then he starts down the back of the row to look at the back of the men's uniforms and equipment. And he said,
the colonel said, and we could all hear him because he was a
very commanding voice, and he said, "all right now men listen
up very carefully. I'm going to give a command, I'm going to
say, raise right foot, and when you prepare then, and then I
say raise, why you all pick up your right foot and point it
towards the back." You understand?

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:Yeah.

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:Okay. So he slowly walked down the line with his hands
behind his back and, see we were all down the line watching
all this, and he walks down and looks at the bottom of the
soles of each man's boot, that's what he wanted to see. To
see if any had holes in them. And he says, "all right now
listen up carefully" -- and all of us could see it coming, he
said, "raise left foot, raise!" Well, now, here's a whole
rank of men with their right foot up in the air, and he says,
"raise left foot, raise," and to my everlasting day, to a man
they fell flat on their face. (Laughter) Everybody knew it
was coming. He never got them to put their foot down before
he said raise left foot. And though all went______ a whole
big row just falling. It was hilarious. And he was really
upset. He finished the full inspection -- the foot
inspections then. (Laughter)

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p:
Q:Did you keep a personal diary at all when you were
overseas?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:I wrote a lot of letters. And my parents certainly saved
all my letters, and I still have them. It's funny, when I
first went in the Marine Corps I said to myself, you know,
this is probably going to be a very intense experience, try
to remember as much of it as you can as you are living it,
and I did. I really did try to salt things away and, as I
say, it's, well, it started 56 years ago. I still -- I can
recapture almost everything pretty well. So, yeah, the diary
is in my head.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p:
Q:When you returned from China and from Korea, what did you
do in like the first days and weeks when you got home?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:When I got back from China the ship brought me all the way
back through the Panama Canal again. I went through the
Panama Canal twice going both ways. That's a long trip. You
take it by ship it's about a month. And I landed in Norfolk
and he then went too Camp Lajeune and then eventually got
discharged down there. And my parents still lived in the
Washington D.C. area then. And because my father had been
overseas in the war, he was in China too, but a different
part of China. But his -- when the war ended his work over
there terminated in about December of '45, he flew home. As
a matter of fact, his plane must have flown over my ship, I
didn't see it, but I hadn't seen my father in several years
then. So when I got home it was a great reunion with him and of course my mother and sister. And when I came back from
Korea I came back to San Francisco, and flew on a plane, and
my parents and sister met me at the National Airport up here.
They lived in Alexandria by that time. And the first few
weeks just -- of course when I came back from Korea I was
still on active duty in the Marine Corps I got stationed at
Quantico. I came back in April and I was stationed up there
and I didn't get out, released until August. And then I
remarried, I got married again to a woman I had gone with
before I had known my first wife, so we got back together.
And she is the mother of my children. Unfortunately, she
died about 26 years ago. So I've had -- I've been made a
widower three times. And my last wife, you may have heard
of, was Susan Hanna (ph), who was the chairman of the English
department here.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:Oh.

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:And in fact there's a scholarship named after her, and she
died of cancer in 1994. So my present wife, a lot of people
told her you better take a good physical before you marry
him.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p:
Q:Where did you go to school for both your under graduate
and your graduate degrees?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:I did my under graduate work at St. John's College in
Annapolis, Maryland; and as I say, it was interrupted by my
World War II service, and I came back and finished there. And when I got out in '53 I went to the University of
Virginia in Charlottesville and spent five years there in
grad school.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:And then you came here to work right after?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:Yes. In fact Mary Washington was part of the University
of Virginia then, you know.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:Yeah, it was.

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:It was a women's college. And the people in the
philosophy department over at Virginia were kind of upset
that Mary Washington didn't have any Virginia philosophers in
it. And the people here wanted to get somebody from Virginia,
so the whole thing was arranged by the chairman here and the
chairman there, and I got my Phd and came over.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q: Let me just change the tape.

div2.note: End of Side 1. Tape Number AFC 2001/001/177.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p:
Q:Did you make any close friendships while you were in the
service?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:As I said, I have still -- in fact I have several close
friends, one who lives down in West Morland (ph) County, who
sent all of his sons to Mary Washington because I was on the
faculty here, and I'm still pretty close to him. I had one
of the lieutenants, in fact I mentioned in my Bronze Star the
raid that it was a two platoons in the assault, he had one of
the other platoons. He was very badly wounded. And he and I still are very close. In fact, he's been in that chair in
the last few weeks. And he sent a couple of his sons here
too. So in fact, his youngest son Holmberg's (ph) his name,
is a columnist for the Richmond Times-Dispatch and he went to
Mary Washington, graduated from Mary Washington, was a
student of mine at the college. Was one of the -- played on
the very early Mary Washington basketball teams. He is 6
foot 8 this guy, and he's been a columnist for the Richmond
Times-Dispatch now for about 10, 15 years, but his dad and I
are still very close.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:And did you join the veterans organizations at all?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:Yeah. I joined the Veterans of Foreign Wars and took out a
life membership many many years ago. I've never been active
in it. I don't go to meetings, but I've -- you know, I like
to ______ (1 second). I am fairly active in the 1st Marine
Division, which is a unit I was in, has an association, and
has a Virginia chapter, and I'm fairly active in that. I'm
also right now very active, and in fact I'm working on my
computer right now, that there's a Fredricksberg area
veterans council, which is a combination of all the units in
the whole region here, who are in the process of raising
money, and we're building a war memorial here in the city.
I'm the recorder or secretary of that organization. So I
am -- I'm pretty active as a veteran, yeah.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:How would you say your military experience influenced how you think about the war and the military in general?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:Well, I'm not an aggressive war monger by any means at
all, I was a philosopher too. I think that my, oh boy, I
don't know how to put this, I have had great respect for
conscientious objectors, and I always have, and I've known a
number. Because several of the coremen (sic) who I was in combat
with in Korea were conscientious objectors, and they were
very brave men, but would not shoot somebody; and I really
respect that. At the same time, I myself am not a
conscientious objector. War is hell, and I really know that.
But we have to at times, and in the present situation we're
in right now, I think at times we have to take whatever steps
are necessary to at the same time recognizing that not
everybody may feel that way.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p:
Q:Since you brought up what is happening right now, what is
your current take on what's happened over in Afghanistan?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:Well, you know, I don't think we know very much about
what's happening. I'll tell you this, I was on the campus
here at Mary Washington all through the Viet Nam war and I
was still going on active duty three months every year. In
fact, most of all through Viet Nam I was an instructor at
Quantico in the summer time and I probably instructed almost
every captain and major either before he went to Viet Nam or
right after he came back. I was a Lieutenant Colonel then.
I had a lot of people that were students of mine that were killed in Viet Nam. And in fact I asked the marine corps to
try to get me back on full time active duty then to go there,
but, the then president of Mary Washington told me that he
wouldn't save my job if I went voluntarily. So I -- and I
was about to be promoted to full professor, and it would have
screwed everything up with the college if I had left, so I
didn't go. But I was still going three months every year. I
had real reservations, as a lot of us did about the war. But
at the same time because I had personal involvement in it I
supported certainly the people that had to fight there, and I
did not, and I was not a war protestor at all. And I was one
of the few people on the faculty who wasn't. So I was kind
of lonely for a while with Viet Nam. In the present
situation I feel that I hope we're doing the right thing. My
main concern is that there's -- I think there's not enough
attention being paid to the reasons why there are literally
millions of people over there who are not supporters
necessarily of Bin Laden, they are not fundamental extremist
Muslims, but they really don't like the United States. And
the maine (sic) source of that, I'm afraid, is that I don't
think -- I think our policy in Israel, particularly the more
recent Israeli governments, I think we really have to
reexamine our policy there. I'm a supporter of the State of Israel, always have been. In fact one of my college
classmates left college and went over there and fought in the war of liberation (sic) in '48. And eventually he stayed in the
reserve army there, and in the '67 war he was a general, an
Israeli general. But they -- I just think that the
Palestinians really do have a gripe, and I think we have to
recognize that. And I think a lot of people in Israel
recognize it, but unfortunately the political realities
there, that the government there ________ (1 second) and it's
what it's doing it's turning off millions of people in the
middle east against America, for no good reason, really. And
I wish there was more sensitivity to that. At the same time
I think whoever, if we can determine who did this to us, I
think it's got to be -- that person has to be brought to
justice. I hope it doesn't involve going to war with anybody,
but I mean we have to bring that person to justice.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p: Q:Anything else you want to add that hasn't been covered?

sp.speaker: George van Sant
sp.p:
A:Oh, I can go on. I just would like to say that I -- and
you say you have a friend in the Marine Corps. The Marine
Corps is a -- and it so happens we're celebrating our
birthday this weekend, it's really a fine organization. I
was never confronted with anything both in China and in Korea
that I hadn't been trained.

sp.speaker: Jan Feldman
sp.p:
Q:Sounds good. I would like to thank you for allowing me to
interview you.
